[Dk 42-198] In pursuance of an order of this Court, made in the above stated cause, bearing date December 4th, 1916, whereby it was referred to the subscriber, one of the special masters of this Court, to ascertain and report, as to the truth of the allegations of the petitioner's petition and his opinion thereon. 

I do report that I have been attended by Wilber A. Heisley, Esq. the solicitor of the said petitioner and in his presence I have taken the depositions of witnesses produced before me and have examined the matters thereby referred to me. 

I find and report that the petitioner and the said defendant were lawfully married in Hackensack, New Jersey on June 14, 1911 and lived together in Buffalo, New York State, until July 1916,

KIMBERLY V. KIMBERLY 

。 when the petitioner left the defendant and took up her residence with her father, at East Orange, New Jersey, where she has since lived: that the petitioner was a bona fide resident of this State at the time of the filing of the petition in this cause. 

I further report that in my opinion, the said marriage has not been consummated between the parties; that the marriage has not been consummated because of the inability of the defendant to consummate it; that the inability on the part of the defendant to consummate the marriage is due to his being incurably impotent at the time of and since his marriage. I find that the petitioner was ignorant of the defendant's impotency at the time of her marriage to him and that she has never ratified said marriage. 

The testimony of the medical witnesses establishes with the petitioner's testimony and that of her father and mother, the facts above found and the petitioner's testimony as to the facts and defendant's admission to the petitioner's father, is in my opinion and I so find, corroborated as to the facts so admitted, by the refusal of the petitioner, at my request, to submit to a physical examination. This request I made known to the solicitor of the petitioner, when the case was first brought to my attention by him. There is no power to issue an order for an examination of the defendant out of the State and under the law of New York State physicians can only testify as to their professional knowledge upon an express waiver of the patient whose privilege is absolute unless waived. I have examined the unreported opinion of Vice 

Chancellor Emery in Benz v. Benz, and this case in my opinion is controlled by that. In that case it was held that the defendant's refusal to comply with an order of the Court for a physical examination constituted sufficient corroboration to sustain a decree on the testimony of the complainant as to the impotence. As a matter of corroboration it is immaterial whether the refusal is to submit to an examination when ordered by the Court, or a refusal, absolute in character, after knowing that the charge made against the defendant is that of incurable impotency-on principle the refusal in each case has the same effect as corroboration. 

I further report, that I am of opinion that all the material facts charged in the petitioner's petition are proven and that she is entitled to a decree annulling her marriage to the defendant and should be permitted to resume her maiden name.

NOCENTI V. RUBERTI 

1145 

DIOMIRA A. NOCENTI, otherwise RUBERTI, petitioner, V. 

JOSEPH P. RUBERTI, defendant. 

[Decided October 6, 1933. Dk 90-150] 

Messrs. Carey & Lane, solicitors for petitioner and exceptant.

FALLON, V. C. 

This matter is before the court on exceptions to Special Master's report pursuant to Rule 113. I have concluded, as a result of my consideration of the matter sub judice, that the exceptions to the Special Master's report should be sustained, and that the prayer of the petitioner that the marriage between her and the defendant be decreed null and void for the cause set forth in the petition should be granted. I will advise a decree accordingly. The proofs in the case satisfactorily manifest, in my judgment, that the defendant induced the petitioner to marry him upon the promise and agreement that within a year thereafter he would marry her according to the rites of the Roman Catholic Church of which both petitioner and defendant are communicants. I deem it unnecessary for the purpose of the matter sub judice to comment upon the proofs herein, or the report of the Special Master with reference thereto other than to say that it appears that the petitioner and the defendant went through a civil marriage ceremony on May 11, 1930, which was performed by a Justice of the Peace, with the understanding and on the express promise of the defendant that he would subsequently have a religious marriage ceremony performed according to the rites of the Roman Catholic Church of which both the petitioner and the defendant are communicants. There is ample corroboration in the proofs to satisfy me that the defendant prevailed upon petitioner to go through a civil marriage ceremony with him upon his promise that he and the petitioner would subsequently be married according to the rites of the church of which both are communicants. The proofs manifest that notwithstanding her entreaty that he comply with his promise in such respect, he refused so to do. The parties did not publicly announce their marriage, nor did they make same known to their friends or acquaintances. In Cox v. Cox, 110 At. 924, Vice-Chancellor

Stevenson held that an unconsummated marriage, which is effected by fraud of any kind whatsoever which would render a contract voidable, is voidable at the option of the injured party, if promptly disaffirmed before any change of status has occurred. 

No change of status has occurred in the matter sub judice. Where,

NOCENTI V. RUBERTI 

as in the case sub judice, a man as an inducement for a woman to enter into a civil marriage ceremony with him, which for reasons of their own they wished to keep secret for a time, promised he would thereafter go through a religious marriage ceremony with her according to the rites of the Roman Catholic Church of which both were communicants, his subsequent refusal to have such religious ceremony performed was fraud upon her for which this court should decree annulment of the marriage, upon her prayer therefor, and particularly where as in the instant case the marriage was not consummated. It is manifest from the proofs herein that if it were not for the aforesaid representation made by the defendant to the petitioner that if she consented to have a civil marriage ceremony performed that a religious marriage ceremony would follow, she would not have entered into marriage with him. It is a general rule that every misrepresentation of a material fact, made with the intention to induce another into an agreement, and without which such other would not have done so, justifies the court in annulling the agreement. Ysern v. Horter, 91 N. J. Eq. 

189 at pp. 192, 193. In Bollmer v. Edsall, 98 N. J. Eq. 299, at page 300, it was held that since the status of marriage is conferred by contract, and since for voiding contracts equity has jurisdiction over all questions of fraud, this court, in an appropriate case, would pronounce such marriage void. See Carris v. Carris, 24 N. J. Eq. 516. See also Vanderbilt v. Mitchell, 72 N. J. Eq. 

910 at p. 918. In Bollmer v. Edsall, supra, it was held that the 

Court of Chancery under its general power to annul fraudulent contracts, has jurisdiction to annul a contract of marriage for sufficient fraud. What is sufficient fraud must be considered and determined in each particular case. I am of the opinion that in the case sub judice there is manifest sufficient fraud to warrant the annulment of the unconsummated marriage of the petitioner and defendant herein, and that such annulment will not be "against sound considerations of public policy." See Ysern v. Horter, supra at p. 204. A number of New York cases, although based upon code provisions, have held that where a wife consented to enter into a civil marriage ceremony on the husband's promise to subsequently have a Hebrew religious ceremony performed, and the husband thereafter absolutely refused to do so the wife was entitled to a decree annulling the marriage, it appearing that she had never cohabited with the husband. Watkins v. Watkins, 107 App. Div. 

489, 189 New York Supp. 860; Rubinson v. Rubinson, 181 New 

York Supp. 28; Rozsa v. Rozsa, 191 New York Supp. 868. Such cases clearly indicate the tendency to relieve an innocent party from marriage contracts induced by fraudulent representations.

NOCENTI V. RUBERTI 

1147 

In my judgment the rule of law as stated in such cases is applicable and should be applied to the case sub judice. It appears to me from the proofs herein that the petitioner would not have consented to the marriage ceremony conducted by a Justice of the Peace if she had known that a material representation, entering into the reason for her consent therefor, that is, a religious ceremony to follow the civil ceremony, was untrue, and I know of no good reason for excepting a marriage contract from the general rule. In Parsons on Contracts, Vol. 2 (8th Ed.) 895, it is said- "If the fraud be such that, had it not been practiced, the contract would not have been made, or the transaction completed, then it is material to it; . . .' In Domschke v. Domschke, 122 N. Y. 

Supp. 892, the court said "Here the marriage has not been consummated, and I see no reason why it should not be annulled, and, if that relief be not afforded, plaintiff will be obliged to waive her religious scruples and consummate the marriage without the promised religious ceremonial marriage, or remain bound to the defendant and deprived of the free right she had to marry according to her religion or to remain single. Where the marriage has not been consummated, it has been held that it is so inchoate and incomplete that the status of the parties is similar to that of parties to an executory contract, and it may be annulled without violating any considerations of public policy." In Ysern v. Horter, supra (at p. 202), Vice-Chancellor Stevenson quoted from Nels. D. & S. 

Sec. 605 as follows:-"Before consummation, the parties stand upon almost the same footing as the parties to an ordinary fraud. 

Where there has been no consummation, any fraud which would be sufficient to annul a contract should in reason be sufficient to annul a marriage ceremony. No satisfactory reason of the law will justify the courts in declaring valid such a contract of marriage when tainted with fraud or duress, where the only effect will be the punishment of the innocent and the confiscation of his or her property by the deception. If the marriage is declared valid, it will exist in name only, preventing both parties from marrying again and bringing the marriage relation into disrepute. Every reason for relief from fraud is applicable here, where a denial of relief is fraught with evil consequences much greater than those flowing from ordinary contracts." Such I consider to be particularly applicable to the case sub judice.

HAUENSTEIN V. HAUENSTEIN MALWINE HAUENSTEIN, now MALWINE SHARP, petitioner, V.

WILLIAM HAUENSTEIN, defendant. 

[Decided September 21, 1933. Dk 57-92] 

William L. Brunyate, Solr. for Defendant-Petitioner.

Edward Stover, Solr. for Petitioner. 

FRANCIS CHILD, A. M. 

The above named petitioner obtained a final decree of divorce from the above named defendant, by a decree entered in the Court of Chancery on or about the 1st day of November, 1925. Previous to the entry of the aforesaid final decree, an order had been made. by this court, directing the defendant to pay to the petitioner, for her support and maintenance, the sum of $20.00 per week, which sum was paid by the defendant down to the date of the application to set aside that portion of the decree or order providing for alimony, the ground of said application being that the petitioner had remarried.

The application for setting aside the alimony is based upon an act of the Legislature of the state of New Jersey, passed in 1933, modifying or amending the 25th Section of the act entitled "An 

Act Providing for Divorces and Decrees of Nullity of Marriage and for Alimony and the Maintenance of Children," P. L., New 

Jersey 1907, page 474. The 25th Section of the aforesaid act was supplemented or amended, by adding thereto the following: "Provided, however, that it shall be unlawful for the Court of Chancery to make any order or decree touching the alimony of the wife, should she have married subsequent to the decree of divorce; and provided, however, that the Court of Chancery upon application of the former husband, on notice and upon proof of the marriage of the former wife after the decree of divorce, must modify any order or decree touching the alimony of the former wife by vacating and annulling any and all provisions in any such order or decree, or both, directing the payment of money for the support of the former wife." 

The purpose of the Legislature in passing this law is plain, it was to avoid the effect of the decisions in the cases of Warren v. 

Warren, 92 N. J. Equity 334; Dietrick v. Dietrick, 99 N. J. Equity 

711; Cropsey v. Cropsey, 104 N. J. Equity 187, which cases held

HAUENSTEIN V. HAUENSTEIN 

1149 that the remarriage of the divorced wife did not, of itself, terminate her right to alimony.

The act of 1933 is perfectly clear. It prohibits an allowance to a divorced wife who remarries and if the allowance has been made, makes it mandatory upon this court to vacate any provision for alimony. A fair construction of the act, leads me to believe that it was the intention of the Legislature that it should apply to all former wives, irrespective of whether they remarried before or after its enactment.

The question to be determined is whether the Legislature had the right to pass such a law which, in the present case, has the effect of cutting off the alimony of the former wife of the defendant, she admittedly having married a man named William E. 

Sharp on January 18, 1931. Sharp deserted her on or about 

August 15, 1931, and died on or about May 1, 1932, before the act in question was passed. 

It is urged upon behalf of the divorced wife that the law in question does not affect her right to alimony because, first, it is an ex post facto law, and second, that it impairs the obligation of a contract and deprives the former wife of a right which existed at the time of its enactment, for which reasons it is claimed that the law in question is unconstitutional because of the provisions of 

Article 3 of Paragraph 7 of the Constitution of New Jersey of 

1844. 

The contention that this law is ex post facto may be readily disposed of as "ex post facto" as used in our constitution has been held to be limited to statutes of a criminal or penal nature. 

In the case of Moore v. The State, 43 N. J. Law 203. Justice 

Dixon, at page 214, said: "But it has long been settled that as used in our Constitutions the phrase embraces only retrospective laws of a criminal or penal character. Blackstone defines an ex post facto law as follows: 'When if an action (indifferent in itself) is committed, the Legislature for the first time declares it to have been a crime and inflicts a punishment upon the person who has committed it.''

The law in question applies to a civil proceeding and, consequently, is not in contravention of the constitutional prohibition against ex post facto laws. 

As to the fact that the act is unconstitutional because it impairs the obligation of a contract, it is sufficient to say that an order of the Court of Chancery to pay alimony is not a contract. Such

HAUENSTEIN V. HAUENSTEIN 

an order may always be modified or vacated by the court which made it. It has none of the essentials of a simple contract and such contracts, and not the so-called "contracts of record," such as judgments of a court were, in my opinion, the contracts referred to in the constitution. Therefore, in my opinion, the law in question is constitutional. 

There is another question which was not urged by counsel for the wife, but should be commented upon, and that is whether the Court of Chancery has inherent jurisdiction, aside from the statute, to decree alimony; if it has, then that right may not be abridged or abolished by a legislative enactment. In order to intelligently answer this question, it is necessary to examine the origin of alimony.

The Court of Chancery in this state acquired whatever inherent jurisdiction it has, from the jurisdiction of the High Court of Chancery of England inherent in that court prior to the Revolution. The English courts had not jurisdiction over divorces until 

1858, when a court for matrimonial causes was created by Statute 20 and 21 Victoria, Chapter 85. Prior to 1858 divorces in England were only obtainable by a bill in Parliament. It is true that the 

Ecclesiastical Court of England had jurisdiction in matters akin to divorce, but the jurisdiction of the Ecclesiastical Court to dissolve a marriage was based solely upon the fact that the marriage was originally void or voidable. The Ecclesiastical Court apparently also had, in certain cases, the right to grant a divorce from bed and board. It, therefore, appears that the English Court of Chancery never had any jurisdiction in connection with the dissolution of marriages and, hence, our Court of Chancery could not acquire any inherent jurisdiction.

The jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery to dissolve marriages or to annul marriages, is purely statutory and it was not until 1794 that any jurisdiction was vested in the Court of Chancery to grant divorces or decrees of nullity. Prior to that date, apparently, the only remedy open to the person seeking to dissolve the marriage was by an act of the Legislature of this state. The first act vesting in the Court of Chancery jurisdiction over the dissolution of marriages is entitled "An Act Concerning Divorces and 

Alimony," Paterson's Revision of 1800, page 143. Even this act did not vest in the Court of Chancery exclusive jurisdiction over divorces and bills for divorce were frequently passed by the Legislature down to the time of the adoption of the Constitution of 1844, which constitution provided, by Section 7, Article 1, that "No divorce shall be granted by the Legislature." 

Alimony has also been a creature of the statute and acts con-

HAUENSTEIN V. HAUENSTEIN 

1151 cerning the same, subsequent to the Act of 1794, were passed in 1818, P. L. 1818, page 20. Another enactment substantially the same as the 1818 act was passed on February 16, 1820 and remained substantially the same until 1907, when the present Divorce Act was adopted. 

The statutory origin of both divorces and alimony was commented upon by Mr. Justice Pitney in the Court of Errors and 

Appeals in 1902, in the case of Lynde v. Lynde, 64 N. J. Equity 

736, at page 751, where he said: "Alimony, in its origin, was the method by which the spiritual courts of England enforced the duty of support owed by the husband to the wife, during such time as they were legally separated pending the marriage relation. . . . At the common law a divorce from the bond of matrimony was granted by the ecclesiastical courts only for such causes as rendered the marriage void ab initio. Naturally, alimony was not allowed as an incident to such a divorce, for, there being no marriage, the duty of maintenance had not been undertaken. . 

Divorces a mensa et thoro, however, amounting merely to a legal separation, were granted for causes which rendered it improper or impossible for the parties to live together, and in such case the ecclesiastical court ordered a periodical allowance to be paid by the husband to the wife for her support, the amount thereof being settled at the discretion of the judge in view of all the circumstances of the case, taking into consideration especially the wife's needs and the husband's means. The spiritual courts reserved and exercised the power of varying the amount of the alimony, from time to time, as required by change of circumstances. Divorces from the bond of matrimony were not granted by the ecclesiastical courts on the ground of adultery or for any other cause which supervened the marriage. For such causes, however, divorces were granted by act of parliament. In this state the subject matter of divorce having been, by statute, committed to the court of Chancery, and causes for absolute divorce having been allowed other than such as rendered the marriage void ab initio, there followed, as a logical consequence, the allowance of permanent alimony in cases of absolute divorce, as a means of enforcing the continuing duty of support which the husband owed to the wife, and of which he was not permitted to absolve himself by his own misconduct, although that misconduct resulted in a dissolution of the marriage."

In view of the fact that it clearly appears that the entire jurisdiction of our Court of Chancery over divorce and alimony is created by statute, it necessarily follows that the Legislature may limit or even take away the jurisdiction so conferred. This court has no right to criticize or take exception to the wisdom of the Legislature in passing such an act, nor can the court take into consideration that in particular cases hardship may be worked by such an act. It is the duty of the court to construe acts of the 

Legislature and if such acts are constitutional and do not infringe or impair the inherent jurisdiction of this Court, the court has no alternative but to accept the same. 

There will be a decree vacating the order or decree for alimony, in accordance with the application made by the defendant husband.

WILLIAM M. HANNA, petitioner, V.

HELEN HANNA, defendant. 

[Dk 91-214] 

JOHN WINANS, Esquire for Petitioner. 

LOUIS RUDNER, Esquire for Defendant. 

ROGERS, A. M. 

Petitioner seeks an absolute divorce from his wife, charging that she has wilfully, continuedly and obstinately deserted him since July 7, 1930. The petition was filed July 13, 1932. 

The petition also alleges that defendant instituted a suit against petitioner in the Supreme Court of the State of New York for a separation from bed and board of petitioner, and for her maintenance and support, charging him with cruel and inhuman treatment. It is alleged that personal service of process in the suit and the complaint were made upon him on January 22, 1931, in the State of New York, and that thereafter such proceedings were had in the cause that a final judgment was entered therein on February 25, 1932, whereby the cause was dismissed upon the merits. The petition further charges that defendant's suit in New 

York for a judicial separation was brought and prosecuted by her improvidently and in bad faith. 

Defendant denies the desertion. She states that she was compelled to separate herself from her husband because of his extreme cruelty toward her, and further contends that there has not been a two year period of wilful, continuous and obstinate desertion as alleged since July 7, 1930, because her suit for judicial

separation in the Supreme Court of the State of New York was pending therein from January 22, 1931 to February 25, 1932 when judgment was rendered against her in that cause. The defendant counterclaims for an absolute divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty.

Petitioner denies the allegations of the counterclaim, and sets up the decree of the Supreme Court of the State of New York in his wife's suit for judicial separation in bar, alleging that the facts and issues involved in the counterclaim in this court are the same as those determined and tried in the former suit. As a second separate defense, he states that until the commencement of this suit, he earnestly, sincerely and in good faith, invited and urged his wife to return and reside with him after her alleged desertion of him on July 7, 1930, and as a third separate defense charges his wife with having induced and provoked the alleged acts of extreme cruelty which she complains of. 

It appears that the parties were married in the State of New York on March 1, 1906, and that thereafter they cohabited and lived in the State of New York until November, 1923, when they removed to, took up their abode in and became bona fide residents of the Borough of Fair Haven, Monmouth County, this State, where the husband has continued to reside until the commencement of this suit. It is admitted, and it is a fact, that the wife left her husband on July 7, 1930, shortly thereafter removing to the City of New York, where she has resided separately substantially ever since.

A duly authenticated copy of the record of the wife's former suit was placed in evidence, together with a like copy of the record of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, upon her appeal from the decree in that suit; which appeal, upon the wife's default, was dismissed on the husband's motion. From this record, it appears that the husband, the defendant therein, was personally served with process within that jurisdiction, and filed an answer to the complaint. The suit is for separation from bed and board of the defendant, and for her reasonable support and maintenance. The complaint alleges cruel and inhuman treatment over a period of three years prior to July 7, 1930. The specifications of the treatment complained of are set forth in detail in the complaint, and enlarged upon to include the period from 1916 to date in the sworn bill of particulars and the sworn amendment to the bill of particulars contained in the record. The judgment of the court dismisses the complaint of the plaintiff upon the merits, and adjudicates that the court has jurisdiction over the cause of action by reason of the facts

that the parties were married within that State, and that the plaintiff was a resident thereof when the action was commenced and continued to be such resident until the time of trial, and that summons was personally served upon the defendant within that State, and that the defendant therein duly appeared and filed his answer. The judgment further refers to the findings of fact, conclusion of law and decision in said cause, which appear as part of the authenticated record. The findings of fact state generally that defendant did not treat plaintiff in a cruel or inhuman manner, and commit acts of violence upon plaintiff, and specifically finds that a number of the alleged acts never took place, and that a number of the alleged acts, though they may have occurred, did not cause the wife to become hysterical, to suffer pain or mental anguish. The conclusions of law are that the plaintiff failed to sustain the allegations of her complaint of cruel and inhuman treatment of her by the defendant, and failed to sustain her allegations that defendant's conduct was such that it might render it unsafe and improper for her to cohabit with him, and finally that the defendant was entitled to judgment, and that the complaint of the plaintiff should be dismissed upon the merits. 

It is strenuously urged by the wife that this adjudication is not dispositive of her right to prove the same facts in support of her claim for relief under the counterclaim, and that she may also offer the same facts in evidence as a defense to petitioner's charge of desertion against her. It is urged with equal determination by the petitioner that the decree of the Court of the State of New York operates as an estoppel to proof of extreme cruelty arising from the same facts under her counterclaim, and bars her defense in that respect as well.

The record in the former suit conclusively shows that the acts of alleged extreme cruelty set forth in the counterclaim in this suit are identical, and it is not seriously contended otherwise. 

The Supreme Court of the State of New York had jurisdiction over both the parties and the subject matter. The defendant was personally served with process within the jurisdiction, and actively defended the same to the point where the appeal was dismissed in his favor. The suit was brought under the New York Civil Practice Act, Sections 1161-1165, which gave the Court jurisdiction over the cause of action by reason of the marriage of the parties in New York, and the plaintiff's residence there at the time of commencement of the suit, and thence to the hearing of the same. 

Pursuant to that statute, a judgment may be entered separating the parties from bed and board forever, or for a limited time, for several causes, inclusive of cruel and inhuman treatment of

the plaintiff by the defendant, or such conduct on the part of the defendant towards the plaintiff as may render it unsafe and improper for the former to cohabit with the latter. The wife in this case pleaded those grounds. Obviously, full faith and credit must be given to a subsisting judgment of a Court of competent jurisdiction of a sister State. No charge is made by the wife that the judgment in the New York Court was in any wise procured by fraud. Feickert v. Feickert, 98 N. J. Eq. 444; 131 Atl. 576.

The doctrine of res judicata has been clearly defined in this 

State, and oft repeated: "All that is necessary is that the right to relief in one suit shall rest upon the same point or question which, in essence and substance, was litigated and determined in the first suit, and in such a case the parties and those in privity with them are concluded, 'not only as to every matter which was offered and received to sustain or defeat the claim or demand, but as to any other admissible matter which might have been offered for that purpose.' In re Walsh's Estate, 80 N. J. Eq. 565, at page 

569; City of Paterson v. Baker, 51 N. J. Eq. 57; Cromwell v. 

Sac County, 94 U. S. 351-52; 24 L. Ed. 195.” "All that is required in cases where the prior and subsequent litigations involve different things, to render the judgment in the first conclusive upon the parties in the subsequent, is that there shall be substantial identity in the subject matter of the two, and that must always be the case, as is obvious, where the judgment in the first rests on a decision of the same question substantially which is presented for decision by the subsequent." 

City of Paterson v. Baker (supra).

The facts upon which relief is based in the case at bar are identical with those pleaded and tried in the former suit. The parties are the same.

The character of relief sought in the former suit is substantially that of a limited divorce as provided for under our statute. Kyle v. Kyle, 52 N. J. Eq. 701; Reibesehl v. Reibesehl, 106 N. J. Eq. 32; 149 Atl. 823; Lake v. Lake, 80 N. J. Eq. 350.

These cases recognize and seemingly enforce decrees obtained under the very statute now under consideration. To grant relief upon the counterclaim, or for her defense to be valid, the husband's treatment must amount to extreme cruelty. 

In the former suit the New York statute required that his alleged conduct toward her must amount to cruel and inhuman treatment, and that it must be such as to render it unsafe and improper for her to cohabit with him. The judgment of the court in the

former suit is then that the husband's conduct did not amount to cruel and inhuman treatment, and that it was not unsafe and improper for her to cohabit with him. The statutes of the various 

States prescribe various grounds for relief under the marital contract. Generally, however, they center about several well recognized grounds. Of these causes, probably adultery is the only one which is couched in the same descriptive terms. Desertion and cruelty are variously described in the statutes. The sole test as to the question of identity of grounds for relief under our statute and those of a sister State is not to be limited to identical descriptive language. Rather, it is what the language of the stated grounds for relief in the statutes under consideration actually connotes. Recourse must be had to the definitions by proper judicial tribunals of these grounds to determine their application to any cause.

It is unnecessary to repeat here what treatment our courts have stated is extreme cruelty. Sachse v. Sachse, 107 N. J. Eq. 41; 

151 Atl. 744. In dealing with the subject of cruelty in the various 

States, it has been said: "But cruelty as used in divorce law has generally been defined by our courts as actual, personal violence, or conduct causing a reasonable apprehension of it, or such a course of treatment as endangers life, limb, or health, and renders cohabitation unsafe." 19 C. J. 44.

In New York State it has been determined that the words "unsafe and improper," (in the very statute invoked by the wife in her former suit), necessarily imply cruelty, and that cruel and inhuman treatment prescribed in said statute means actual, personal violence, menaces or threats creating reasonable apprehension of bodily harm. Umbach v. Umbach, 183 App. Div. 495; 171 

NYS, 138; Mason v. Mason, 1 Edw. 278; Donohue v. Donohue, 180 App. Div. 361; 167 NYS, 715; Perry v. Perry, 2 Paige 501.

Can there be any substantial distinction made between these definitions of the grounds for relief under these statutes? If not, then it must be held that the Supreme Court of the State of New York in the wife's former suit adjudicated, upon the facts presented and pleaded, that the husband was not guilty of any extreme cruelty by reason of his alleged treatment of her. Of course, were there a substantial distinction between the grounds for relief in the New York statute and ours, then the application of the adjudication in the former suit, would be limited to the findings of the New York State Court as to the happening, or not,

of the specific acts complained of in the case at bar. The application of the doctrine of res judicata cannot be avoided by changing the relief prayed for. O'Brien v. O'Brien, 103 N. J. Eq. 214; 

142 Atl. 898; affirmed 105 N. J. Eq. 250; 147 Atl. 911. The wife's former suit, and her counterclaim are suits for divorce. 

I hold that the judgment in the former suit is a complete bar to the production of the same facts in evidence in the suit at bar urging that they amount to extreme cruelty under our statute. 

They cannot be the basis for relief under the wife's counterclaim. 

She is estopped by the judgment of the sister State from relief upon the ground of extreme cruelty based upon the same acts. 

She is equally estopped from justifying her desertion of the defendant by reason of these same facts, (which are the subject of the judgment in New York State), nor can it be said that these same facts may be put in evidence again because they might justify her desertion of the husband, though they did not amount to extreme cruelty. The law is well settled in our State that the husband or wife is not justified in leaving the other except for a cause, which, in itself, amounts to a matrimonial offense under our statute. Arnaboldi v. Arnaboldi, 101 N. J. Eq. 126; 138 Atl. 116. 

It is urged for the defendant that the ruling in Pearson v. Pearson, 230 N. Y. 141; 129 N. E. 349, should be followed. To my mind that case substantially upholds the principles applied here. 

The sole distinction is in method of application of the bar of the foreign judgment. In that respect, though the result attained is the same, I do not agree with it. The New York Court, in my judgment, failed to give the effect to the foreign judgment which it was bound to, having found identity of issue of law. It preferred, evidently, to apply the judgment upon the facts pursuant to the law as established in New York. 

It is also urged that pursuant to paragraph 33 of our statute the judgment in the former suit should not be considered effective. 

It is pointed out that the suit was based upon a cause of action which arose in this State, and contended that that cause of action was not ground for divorce under our statute. The fact is that the acts pleaded do come within the extreme cruelty ground stated in our statute as has already been observed. The jurisdictional requirements of the New York State statute were fully complied with in the former suit. Our statute gives our court jurisdiction over causes of action which arise in other jurisdictions, provided a definite residence has been acquired in this State, and the laws of the jurisdiction where the cause of action arose

afforded the suitor the same grounds for relief. It would be inconsistent, if it could be properly done, to deny the jurisdiction of foreign courts for this reason, in view of the provisions of our statute under similar circumstances. It may also be observed that the wife could have, under our statute, instituted a suit for separate maintenance in this State. She elected instead to bring her suit in New York State. Reasonably, she should not be permitted now to avoid the effect of the judgment in that suit. Lake v. Lake (supra). However, paragraph 33 of our statute, in my judgment, has no such bearing upon the effect of the New York decree, because in this case there is no evidence that the wife went to New York in order to procure a decree of divorce. That is essential to the application of that section of our statute. Stephens v. Evans, 105 N. J. Eq. 203; 147 Atl. 447.

It is contended, however, that the husband cannot obtain a decree because the time during which the suit in New York State was pending (from January 22, 1931 to February 25, 1932), cannot be computed as part of the desertion period. Accordingly, the desertion having commenced on July 7, 1930, and the suit having been instituted on July 13, 1932, there remains only a desertion of about eleven months after the period of pendency of the former suit is deducted. That is a settled rule of law in this State beyond doubt. There are exceptions, however. The husband charges in this case that the former suit was not instituted by his wife in good faith, but in fraud of the court. He contends that she knew she had no substantial grounds for the relief sought. It is said in Weigel v. Weigel, 63 N. J. Eq. 677, at p. 681: "When, however, it is shown that the wife's previous suit, the pendency of which is set up to excuse her apparent desertion, was based on allegations which were known by her to be false when they were submitted to the court, and when her testimony in that suit, in support of those allegations, is proven to have been untrue by many disinterested witnesses, so that it is made quite clear that her previous suit was a false pretence, and not a genuine presentation of a believed grievance, the excusatory effect of the pendency of the previous suit is wholly lost. Such an exhibition shows that the proceeding was a fraud upon the court, on the law, and on the defendant attacked by it. Its pendency is no answer to proof that the wife wilfully, continuedly and obstinately abandoned her husband. Indeed, it may be additional evidence of the obstinacy of her determination to desert her husband, escape from her marital duty."

Petitioner and defendant offered in evidence a transcript of the testimony taken at the hearing in the former suit of the wife in New York in support of their respective contentions. It was also testified, though denied by the wife, that she had on several occasions in the latter part of 1929 and the early part of 1930 said that she was going to leave her husband as soon as the son had completed his education, and that she no longer wanted to live in Fair Haven. There is evidence that in the fall of 1929 the wife had urged that her husband support her separate and apart from him, and negotiations to that end were almost completed by the husband and wife through their lawyers. At the last moment these negotiations were broken off by the husband. The wife also testified that she would not now return to and live with her husband, and she doubted that she would ever have done so after she had left him on July 7, 1930. She also denied that her husband had personally solicited her return to him shortly before the hearing in January, 1932, in her suit in New York State. The husband testified that he did so. His testimony was corroborated, and her statement is directly contradictory of her answers set forth on page 104 of the transcript of testimony in the New York suit. Numerous efforts on the part of the husband to secure the wife's return were proven to have been made through mutual friends. These efforts were denied substantially by the wife, but 

I am satisfied that such efforts were made, and it is satisfactorily proven that the husband was at all times willing for his wife to return to him at their Fair Haven home, and that that home was open for her return, if she so willed. I am satisfied that the husband made reasonable advances to his wife for her return as he was required to do. However, if his treatment of her was such as justified her leaving him, it was not necessary for her to heed his advances. To return to him would bar her suit and destroy the cause of action accrued in her favor. 

To avoid the prejudicial effect of the pendency of the prior suit upon the desertion period pleaded by the husband in this case, it is necessary that it clearly and convincingly appear from all the evidence that the wife did not prosecute her former suit in good faith. The allegations contained in the complaint, the bill of particulars, the amended bill of particulars and the amendment to the complaint permitted in court at the time of the hearing, if sustained by proof would have amply justified the relief prayed for. The transcript of testimony shows that the wife in some respects contradicted her own testimony. She did, however, testify as to her husband's abusive treatment of her on a number of occasions substantially as the charges were alleged, and particu-

larly as to the occasion immediately prior to her leaving him with the son on July 7, 1930. The husband denied the substance of his wife's testimony in many respects admitted many elements of it and justified much of it by showing that his wife had constantly, and without justification, criticised, nagged and berated. him. He explained away some of her charges by showing provocation. Disinterested witnesses disputed some of the charges she made, and explained incidents complained of so that it appears that she was the aggressor as well as the husband. The happenings on the occasion when she left her husband were substantially corroborated by the son, and it fairly appears that then the father and the son engaged in a heated quarrel. The wife attempted to interfere, and the husband became enraged, with the result that the son and the wife left the home. From the whole of the testimony, I am satisfied that the situation between the husband and wife had become unbearable. It was substantially, however, of their own making-each was at fault. It cannot be said that the wife was clearly and convincingly guilty of bad faith in prosecuting her former suit. In my judgment, she was justified in bringing her suit, though she did not prevail. 

A decree should be entered dismissing the petition and counterclaim.

ROGERS, A. M. 

After conclusions were filed in the above cause holding that the petition and counterclaim should be dismissed, leave was given petitioner to reargue one phase of the matter. I had found that the wife was guilty of a wilful, continuous and obstinate desertion as alleged by the husband in his petition. However, I concluded that the time during which the wife's suit against her husband was pending in the Supreme Court in New York State could not be tolled as part of the period of desertion, and accordingly the husband had not proved a desertion for the statutory term. I determined that the wife's suit had been brought in good faith, and my conclusions filed state the basis of my judgment in

that respect. matter.

The reargument is directed to this phase of the It is now submitted that the charge against the wife, that her former suit was brought in bad faith, is conclusively established because the findings of fact filed by the Court substantially are that the acts of cruelty which she complained of never occurred, and in a few instances, though they may have happened, did not constitute actionable cruelty in New York State. It is insisted that the grounds of the former suit were such inherently that they must have been personally known to the wife, and that from the findings of fact, it is conclusive upon the fact of the record that she knew the falsity of her charges, and that her former suit was practically a fabrication. It is urged that these findings of fact are conclusive upon the parties to this suit for all purposes whatever, and that the wife is as conclusively bound in this respect as I held she was bound by the decree of that Court in that suit in respect to the subject matter of the counterclaim in the case under consideration.

Now the fact is that the question of the wife's good faith in instituting her former suit was raised and put in issue for the first time in this suit by the husband in answer to the wife's defense to the petition charging her with desertion. The wife's good faith was not at any time in issue in the former suit. The findings of fact are silent upon any such issue. The findings of fact and the judgment in the former suit are conclusive upon the parties thereto only in respect to those matters within the issues actually litigated and determined. Nagle vs. Conrad, 96 N. J. Eq. 61; 125 Atl. 20; 

Paterson vs. Baker, 51 N. J. Eq. 49; 26 Atl. 325; and Walsh's 

Estate, 80 N. J. Eq. 565; 74 Atl. 563. The issue of the wife's good faith having been raised for the first time in this suit, I have no hesitation in holding that the parties to this suit are not in that respect conclusively bound by the findings of fact in the record in the former suit, nor is the Court to determine that question solely from those findings. I can come to no other view than that the issue of good faith was properly determined with the aid of the record and the transcript of testimony in the former suit. Weigel vs. Weigel, 63 N. J. Eq. 677; 52 Atl. 1123; affirmed 65 N. J. Eq. 

398; 54 Atl. 1125. Locher vs. Locher, 112 N. J. Eq. 25; 163 Atl. 251.

In my conclusions I stated the evidence before me relating to the question of the wife's good faith in prosecuting her former suit. I held that the wife's fraud upon the Court must be clearly and convincingly proved and I found that measured by that standard, the husband had not sustained his charge. There is little,

CHARNOFSKY V. CHARNOFSKY 

if any, evidence that the wife knew that her charges were false when she instituted her suit and the inconsistencies in her testimony are not such as fairly infer that she knew her charges were false. Vice Chancellor Grey in the Weigel case (supra) from the testimony in the second suit, found an explanation satisfactory to him of the falsity of the wife's charges made in the prior suit and he inferred from that situation that the wife knew her former suit was based upon false charges. It also appeared in that case that many of the most vicious charges were not at all substantiated by the wife in her former suit. Those elements are not present in this cause. Most of the incidents charged were substantiated by the wife. She failed to secure relief because the Court found that as a matter of law the treatment accorded her was not of a sufficient degree to constitute cruelty. With this supplement, the matter will rest as heretofore concluded. 

ANNE CHARNOFSKY, petitioner, V. 

JULIUS J. CHARNOFSKY, defendant. [Dk 99/18] Matthew M. Epstein, Solicitor for petitioner.

ROGERS, A. M. 

This is a suit for absolute divorce on the ground of desertion. 

Upon petitioner's application for an order referring the cause for hearing ex parte on the merits, after defendant's default, it appears that petitioner's affidavit annexed to the petition is as follows: "I am the petitioner in the foregoing petition. My said petition is not made by any collusion between me and the defendant; and the facts, matters and things set forth in said petition, so far as they relate to the acts of the petitioner are true and so far as they relate to the acts of others, she believes them to be true."

The affidavit of "non-collusion" as it has been frequently termed, is a statutory requirement. It must be made by the petitioner, and it must be annexed to the petition. It is necessary in order that the Court of Chancery shall have jurisdiction of any suit for divorce or nullity of marriage under our divorce statute. 

The statutory provision is:

CHARNOFSKY V. CHARNOFSKY 

1163 "The Court of Chancery shall not have jurisdiction of any cause for divorce or nullity of marriage under this act, unless the petitioner shall make his or her oath or affirmation, which shall be annexed to the petition, that his or her petition is not made by any collusion between him or her and the defendant, but in truth and good faith, for the causes set forth in the petition." P. L. 1907, page 477; 2 C. S. 1910, Section 8, page 2032. 

Rule 256a of the Court of Chancery requires that petitions for divorce and nullity of marriage be verified by petitioner and that the verification be added to the statutory affidavit of non-collusion. 

The affidavit in question in that respect complies with the rule. 

However, the statutory phrase "but in truth and good faith for the causes set forth in the petition" was omitted from the affidavit. 

It is urged that the form of the affidavit, nevertheless, substantially complies with the statute and that substantial compliance is sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the Court over the cause of action pleaded. I find no difficulty with the proposition that substantial compliance with the statutory form of the affidavit is sufficient. The sole question is whether the affidavit under consideration constitutes substantial compliance. Brant vs. Brant, 71 Eq. 66, 71 Atl. 350; Welch vs. Welch, 85 Eq. 508. 

The late Chancellor Walker held in Riehl vs. Riehl, 101 Eq. 

15, 137 Atl. 787, that the affidavit of non-collusion in the form required by our statute amounts to a verification of the petition. 

It is there said that the petition could not be made "in truth" unless at least the material allegations therein were true. Reasonably, it may be said then, that the significance of the statutory words "but in truth . . . for the causes set forth in the petition" is equivalent to the statute requiring the petition in such cases to be verified by the petitioner. The affidavit in question contains the verification required by Rule 256a, and that verification supplies the essential meaning of the statutory words "in truth for the causes set forth in the petition." The statute requires that the petitioner's oath shall also state that the petition is made "in . . .. good faith for the causes set forth in the petition." By those words the legislature meant that the petitioner should be required to do more than verify the material allegations of the petition in such cases. Public policy required, in its judgment that it should appear from the oath of the petitioner annexed to the petition that petitioner had in nowise connived at, or consented to the alleged ground for relief, nor been guilty of an uncondoned matrimonial offense, nor had some ulterior purpose or vexatious intent in bringing the suit. Biddle,

CHARNOFSKY V. CHARNOFSKY 

cance.

N. J. Divorce Law (2nd Ed.) page 107. Good conscience cer tainly requires that suits for divorce and nullity of marriage be free from any such taints. The statutory words of petitioner's oath that the petition be made in good faith have that signifi- It cannot be said, in my judgment, that the fair meaning of the preceding part of the oath to the effect that the petition is not made by any collusion between petitioner and the defendant, is inclusive of, and synonymous with, the affirmative statement to the effect that the petition is made in good faith, etc. If the negative statement were synonymous with the affirmative statement, I still believe that there would not be substantial compliance with the statute unless the affidavit stated the proposition, required by the statute to be under oath, both in the negative and the affirmative. In accordance with these views, I hold that the form of the affidavit in question does not constitute substantial compliance with the statutory form. The omission of the words "and in good faith" is fatal. In my judgment a significant part of the statutory phraseology of the affidavit of non-collusion is not contained in the affidavit annexed to the petition in this cause.

I am unable to find any decision of our Courts squarely passing upon the question of amendment of a defective affidavit of noncollusion. A literal reading of Paragraph 8 of the statute admits of no doubt that the affidavit is a prerequisite to jurisdiction in all causes for divorce or nullity of marriage under the statute. Section 19 of our Divorce Act provides that: "No proceedings in any suit commenced under this act shall be set aside or otherwise annulled or made void for any defect in matter of form or for any mistake or omission not affecting the real merits of the cause, and the Chancellor may permit either party to amend his or her proceedings in the cause, either in matters of form or substance and proceed to give judgment according to the merits of the case." 

That section of our statute has been construed many times, and quite liberally, it seems. Succhierelli vs. Succhierelli, 101 Eq. 30; 

137 Atl. 839; Gondas vs. Gondas, 98 Eq. 473, 134 Atl. 615; Fodor vs. Kunie, 92 Eq. 30, 112 Atl. 598; Wallace vs. Wallace, 112 Eq. 

292, 164 Atl. 565. It is true that as a general rule jurisdiction cannot be conferred by amendment. Woodmont Assoc. vs. Town of Milford, 85 Conn. 517, 84 Atl. 307. However, it is well settled that amendment is permissible to supply jurisdictional defects where there is jurisdiction of the subject matter. 49 C. J. 505.

The majority rule clearly seems to favor permitting amendment of affidavits required for jurisdiction to be annexed to initial pleadings in divorce and nullity suits. 19 C. J. 122; Fitzpatrick vs. Fitzpatrick, 131 Tenn. 54, 173 S. W. 444. Jurisdiction to amend is supplied by the section of our statute permitting amendments in form or substance. And that is so though the amendment is to add a jurisdictional element omitted. 

I shall advise an order permitting petitioner to file an amended petition annexed to which there shall be petitioner's affidavit of non-collusion in the form required by our statute.

Herbert WALKER, defendant. [Dk 75-529]
