ROGERS, A. M. 

The wife's petition for divorce from bed and board charging her husband with desertion was filed in November 1929, and was moved for hearing ex parte on the merits in October 1933. The proofs amply substantiate her rights to this relief, and I will advise a decree.

The husband did not answer, but appeared and was represented by counsel at the hearing. He objected to proofs being taken on the alimony phase of the case, contending that he was discharged from further responsibility for maintenance by an order entered in this cause on January 31st, 1931. By that order, he urged, the 

Court had approved an agreement of the parties for maintenance after examining into the circumstances of the parties, and that he had fully performed the order by payment to his wife of the lump sum in lieu of future alimony. The order is as follows: "This matter being opened to the Court by Merritt Lane, solicitor of the defendant, and it appearing that by stipulation entered in this cause on January 15, 1930, it was agreed that the complainant would accept as and for a fair and reasonable sum for her maintenance the sum of $50. per week to begin on the date of settlement of the following causes, viz; Between 

Herbert Walker and Elmer L. Walker, complainants, and 

Walker Realty Co., Inc., Elizabeth Walker, C. Herbert Walker

and H. Vivian Walker, defendants; and Between Elmer L. 

Walker, complainant, and Arlington Realty Co., Inc., H. Vivian 

Walker and C. Herbert Walker, defendants;

And it appearing that by order entered this day said causes have been settled and the said Elizabeth Walker has received in lieu of weekly payment of $50. per week the lump sum of $5,200., and in addition thereto has received an assignment of the shares of stock of the Holland Building & Loan Association, West Essex Building & Loan Association and Millford Park 

Building & Loan Association mentioned in said stipulation; 

And it appearing that the said Herbert Walker has fully paid and satisfied by said lump sum payment of all moneys due and to become due from him to the said Elizabeth Walker as and for a fair and reasonable sum for her maintenance; 

It is, on this 31st day of January, 1931, ordered, adjudged and decreed that the said Herbert Walker be, and he hereby is, relieved and discharged of and from all obligation to make any further payments to the said Elizabeth Walker for maintenance."

The wife contended that despite the order she was entitled to have the alimony question gone into under the prayer in the petition urging that the settlement made between the parties was not actually examined into and approved by the Court as reasonable and fair. The objection was taken under advisement, and the proofs on the question of alimony were quite fully taken subject to the disposition of the husband's objection. 

I am satisfied that, when the Court approved the husband's and wife's agreement purporting to finally settle the wife's right to maintenance, it did so after having determined that, in the circumstances of the parties, the arrangement was fair and reasonable to the wife. No testimony was submitted to show otherwise, and in the third paragraph of the recital in the order it states in so many words that it then appeared that the defendant had made the lump sum payment to the petitioner "as and for a fair and reasonable sum for her maintenance." I do not think it is the law that the order must actually adjudge such to have been the fact. It should be sufficient if it appears that the Court sanctioned the settlement arrived at between the parties, and from the order such appears to have been the case here. Defendant's objection to granting further alimony under the prayer of the petition in face of the order of January 31st, 1931, was sustained for the reason that the pleadings presented no issue to the defendant in light of that order, and that order had effectually disposed of

and other der endr ndi the Co ndar he p ned fendi posed W2 the prayer for alimony contained in the petition for divorce. 

Greenberg vs. Greenberg, 99 N. J. Eq. 461. Therein, at p. 469, it is said "The petitioner herein, however, cannot invoke the power of the Court to award alimony in the face of her agreement by merely moving for it. If she desires to press the question, she must file a petition setting forth the facts upon which she relies as showing that she is entitled, under the decisions, to have the question opened and her claim considered. In other words, she must tender an issue to the defendant by proper pleading."

Subsequently, a supplemental petition was filed by leave of Court pursuant to the practice just referred to, defendant answered thereto, and a full hearing was had. It was agreed that the evidence relating to the subject matter of the supplemental petition submitted at the original hearing on the petition for divorce pending the disposition of defendant's then objection, should be considered as taken upon the supplemental petition and answer, and, if further alimony was awarded petitioner, it should commence as of February 7th, 1934. It may be here observed that the hearings were not concluded by the parties until July 1st, last. 

It is necessary, in my judgment, to quite fully relate the facts to properly present the real issue. They are somewhat complicated by the fact that the lump sum settlement of alimony under the order of January 31st, 1931, in this cause, was directly connected with the settlement by consent decree of two other suits in this Court. In one of these suits this husband and a son sued his wife, another son, a daughter and Walker Realty Company, a real estate holding company in which those parties appear to have been interested. The same complainant-son also sued the other son, the daughter, and Arlington Realty Company, a real estate holding company in which it appears these parties were interested. 

Pursuant to agreement between the parties, a decree was entered in these causes, (evidently consolidated for that purpose), which fully settled the rights of all concerned. 

From the proofs submitted it fairly appears that the husband. and wife are about seventy years of age, and that they have been living separate and apart since 1924 and that, prior to the institution of this suit, the husband had been paying his wife the sum of $26.00 per week pursuant to an order of the Essex County 

Relations Court. The wife is unqualified to earn her own living. 

The husband appears to be receiving one salary of about $225.00 per month with maintenance, and another of about $500.00 per

annum. He does not appear to have any other income, though he does own some mortgages and personal property. He is faced with moderate debt, and submits that he is subject to retirement from the position which brings him $225.00 per month and consequential loss of maintenance, and that he may lose his annual salary of about $500.00 as secretary of a Building and Loan Association. It appears that the wife, for some time past, has had no income whatsoever, and has lived on the gratuities of the son and daughter who are no longer able to aid her. She does appear to own practically all the stock in the Walker Realty Company, which holds a large apartment house in the City of Newark. The operations of that company have been conducted at a loss ever since 1931, and the only benefit that the wife has received from it is that she has been permitted to live in its apartment house free of rent. Though the defendant claims petitioner's interest in this company is very valuable, and that the reason for it not producing an income is due to mis-management, such does not appear to be the fact. The defendant has had ample opportunity to substantiate these charges. It does appear that the apartment property is heavily mortgaged, and that the Walker Realty Company has operated it for some time past upon the mortgagee's terms. It likewise appears that the wife's interest in Arlington 

Realty Company has brought her no income since 1931, and that she was forced to give up her interest in that concern, (also a real estate holding company owning an apartment house in Avon-by the Sea), due to the fact that she was financially unable to meet existing corporate indebtedness so that it might continue to operate. Her son now substantially owns that corporation, and it appears that it has produced no net income for some time past, but has been conducted at a considerable loss. It also appears that there is no income available to the petitioner from any Florida property in which she may be interested. There is a property there owned by Broadmoor Realty Company. The wife has but one share of stock in that corporation. It is substantially owned by the son and the daughter. The property has been closed for several years until this past winter, when it produced a rental considerably less than the taxes and repairs. 

It is admitted that the wife did not actually receive $5,200.00 in cash from the lump sum settlement, but that her husband credited that amount for her benefit against the sum he received under the terms of settlement of the property suits herein before referred to between these parties and their children. It also appears that the wife expended the cash proceeds, amounting to $1,589.02 received from the Building and Loan Association shares turned

over to her under the lump settlement, in satisfaction of existing indebtedness of the Walker Realty Company. So much for the facts presently.

The wife's right to alimony is defined by paragraph 25 of our Divorce Act of 1907 (II C. S. 1910, p. 2035). It is allowed her as a means of enforcing a continuing duty of support which the husband owes to the wife, and from which he is not permitted to absolve himself by his own misconduct. It is a purely personal right vested in her and not susceptible of transfer or assignment. 

This Court will not permit her to be precluded from enforcing that right. It will only approve her own agreement as to alimony where, after examination into the circumstances, the arrangement appears to be fair and reasonable; and this applies to an arrangement where alimony is to be paid from time to time as well as to an agreement whereby a lump sum settlement is approved in discharge of any future claim. The import of the statute requires that the matter be kept open to the end that it may be controlled by changing needs and circumstances of the parties. This does not mean that the Court, when requested, will not approve lump sum settlements which, from examination, appear to be fair and reasonable. Such is an established practice, but the efficacy with which such a decreed settlement shall be considered as barring the wife from being entitled to further allowance must always be determined in light of all circumstances surrounding the settlement, the subsequent conduct of the parties in relation to such settlement, and their circumstances at the time of the wife's later application. In such case the wife has a greater burden of proof than upon an original application for maintenance. This proposition is elaborately stated in Greenberg vs. Greenberg (supra), and the authoritative cases in this Court, and in the Court of Errors and Appeals are therein cited. That case is to be distinguished from this because there the parties had been absolutely divorced, and the alimony order was entered upon the agreement of the parties only. This is a suit for limited divorce. The marital status is in no wise altered, and the alimony order was entered with the Court's express approval of the spouse's agreement. 

In Baumgarten vs. Baumgarten, 107 N. J. Eq. 274 the Vice 

Chancellor dealt with a maintenance suit wherein the wife had received a lump sum settlement pronounced fair and reasonable by the Court. The wife applied for a further allowance claiming that she had lost the proceeds of the lump sum settlement, and was in necessitous circumstances. It was observed that the parties were still in the relationship of husband and wife, and that the statutory provision for alimony in such case.

"should be interpreted in the light of the law which fixes upon the husband a continuing duty to support his wife. The policy of our law is illustrated by a supplement to the Crimes Act. 

P. L. 1917, p. 110. A husband who willfully neglects to provide for the support of his wife in necessitous circumstances is denounced as a criminal. I do not think that the statute under which the present suit is brought authorizes the Court to permit the husband to escape his civil liability to provide for his wife so long as he remains her husband. The Court cannot divest itself of the authority and duty to make such further orders touching the support and maintenance of the wife as may be just and equitable. The order of March 21st, 1928, should be interpreted to mean that the payment of the gross sum of $5,000.00 should satisfy the claims of the complainant against the defendant for maintenance only until equity and justice requires the payment of additional sums." 

The Vice Chancellor then determined the application for further allowance upon the financial circumstances of the parties and all the factors effecting the equity of her demand including the manner in which she had expended the proceeds of the lump sum settlement. Her application for alimony pendente lite was denied because the burden cast upon her, by the receipt of the lump sum settlement, was judged to be too great to be overcome by ex parte affidavits. I have examined the file in the Clerk's office in this cause, and find that on final hearing the application was denied in praesenti because the wife had not satisfactorily explained the possibility of recovery of a part of the lump sum settlement which she had loaned to a relative. The appeal instituted in the case does not appear to have been prosecuted. These principles of law control in the case sub judice, and I shall now turn to the substantial defenses offered and the equities. 

In passing upon the defense most strenuously put forward by the husband, I shall have dealt with the most essential equity present. It is urged that the alimony order should not be modified. unless all of the parties to the property suits (heretofore referred to as settled by consent decree), are first made parties of this suit, so that the rights of the husband and wife adjudged by that decree may be adjusted and the decree accordingly modified. It is contended that the consent decree in the property suits, and the order for payment of lump sum alimony in this suit, were based upon stipulation entered into by the husband and wife which were integral parts of an entire agreement, that the stipulations were inseparable, that the husband entered into the stipulation in

the property suits solely to be relieved of his obligation to support his wife in the future, and that the consideration passing to the wife in the property suit by the husband's agreement was substantially in satisfaction of that obligation, as much so as the sum involved in the alimony settlement actually set forth in the order in this cause.

The stipulation entered into by the parties to this suit, relating to the settlement of alimony by payment of a gross sum, recites the existence of this suit and the fact that, contemporaneously, a stipulation was entered into between the parties in the property suits (including these spouses) as a result of which the husband surrendered to the wife rights in certain properties owned by Arlington Realty Company and Walker Realty Company, in consideration of which recitals, the parties determined upon $50.00 per week as a proper sum for the wife's maintenance to begin when the property suits were settled pursuant to the stipulation entered into by the husband and wife and the other parties to those suits, a copy of which stipulation was annexed and made a part of the agreement between the husband and the wife, and which maintenance was to run at that rate for a period of two years. 

It was to cease then, and the husband was to pay the cash surrender value of certain designated shares of Building and Loan Association stock in a lump sum to his wife in lieu of all further alimony. And it was further stipulated that, if the value of these shares of stock was paid, or if the proposed settlement of the property suits was not effected, then the wife was bound to return the certificates of said stock to the husband.

The stipulation in the property suits first compelled the defendants to pay certain fees of a receiver appointed by the Court in those causes together with a stipulated counsel fee to the complainant's counsel as well as all other costs of those proceedings. 

The individual defendants comprising the wife, a son and a daughter, contracted to pay the sum of $27,500.00 to the complainant husband and the complainant son on a definite date in full settlement of, and as payment for, the rights of the said complainants in the Walker Realty Company and the Arlington Realty Company, and the complainants agreed, thereupon, to transfer to the said individual defendants, all of their right, title and interest in the said corporations, as well as to transfer all stock to those individual defendants owned by the complainants. 

There then followed provisions concerning the maintenance of the corporate properties in the interim of settlement under the stipulation, and the defendants agreed to pay all creditors of the corporations before the date fixed for settlement under the stipulation.

The complainants agreed to take a mortgage of $20,000.00 existing upon property of the Arlington Realty Company in lieu of the payment of $18,000.00 in cash, and it was agreed by the parties that the causes should be dismissed, including every appeal taken therein, upon the execution of the stipulation, and that the parties would not take any further appeal from the decree to be entered in the causes. The foregoing stipulation was executed on January 

15th, 1930, and on January 27th, 1930, the decree was entered in the property suits pursuant thereto. 

It is admitted that the husband and the son received satisfaction pursuant to the stipulation in the property suits. It may be inferred that they participated equally. There appears to be no specific proof that the husband surrendered to his wife any of his property rights in the property suits even in partial consideration of being discharged from further duty of his wife. For these stipulations and the resultant decrees, so far as concerns the husband and wife, to be considered as flowing from a single or integral agreement for that purpose, it must appear to be so from the stipulations and decrees themselves. It is apparent, from the alimony stipulation, that it was dependent upon, and was to follow, the execution of the stipulation of the property suits. So far as concerns the question of alimony, there certainly seems to be no other connection with the settlement of the property suits. If there was intended to be such further connection between these stipulations, it could have been (and I am satisfied that it would have been) actually referred to in the alimony stipulation, and in such wise as to constitute it a part of the actual alimony settlement. 

The stipulation in this suit specifically states the terms upon which the parties agreed in order to dispose of the alimony question, and in doing so specifies certain Building and Loan Association stock which was in part the subject of the property suits, thus showing that, as to those items of property, the husband was surrendering his interest therein to the wife in consideration of her consenting to discharge him from responsibility for her support. It would have been as simple a matter to have incorporated in that stipulation, as the moving force in the alimony agreement, any other items which the husband actually surrendered to his wife in consideration for the privilege he was seeking. The recital in the stipulation is in two parts only. First, it refers to the cause in which the subject matter exists, second, it refers to the fact that the stipulation has been entered into by the husband and the wife in the property suits, and the recitals conclude with the phrase “in consideration thereof." That phrase refers to the fact that the stipulation in the property suits had been concluded, wherein, as

that stipulation provides, inter alia, the husband agreed to surrender to his wife his interest in the Arlington Realty Company and the Walker Realty Company. It does not mean that the stipulation in the property suits so far as the husband was concerned in any wise constituted settlement of his obligation to support his wife in accordance with their agreement. It is evident that the husband and the wife were ready to agree on the question of settlement of alimony by a lump sum payment only when the property suits had been disposed of by agreement. And this is the more evident because the alimony settlement, under the stipulation, was made dependent upon the actual execution of the stipulations in the property suits by the parties thereto. Necessarily the 

Court adjudged the fairness of the alimony settlement in light of the wife's estate as it was after the settlement of the property suits. 

By that settlement it appeared as she admits in the supplemental petition, that she was expectantly in a fair position to maintain herself. But that does not mean that the alimony agreement as approved really included the arrangement whereby the husband was to vest his property rights in his wife. That was a separate matter, separately concluded, as a result of which the husband was paid off, and following and in light of which the alimony arrangement was concluded and approved by the Court. 

If there could be any question on this point, it must be resolved against the defendant because of the recitals contained in the order for alimony in this cause of January 31st, 1931, which was prepared and presented to the Court by the husband's solicitor. 

There is no reference therein to any surrender of rights by the husband to the wife in the property suits constituting a part of the consideration for discharging the husband from further obligation to support his wife. In that respect, that order discharging the husband is based entirely upon the settlement of cash and the value of the shares of, Building and Loan Association stock as itemized in the stipulation between the parties in this suit in view of the circumstances of the parties and their then separate estates. 

In my judgment, the property rights acquired by the wife in the property suits constituted her separate property, and will be dealt with as such herein so far as they exist today. I perceive that the separate estate of a wife and her personal right to maintenance from her husband, are co-existent. One is not dispositive of the other, though usually the amount of alimony is measured in light of the availability of the wife's separate estate for her maintenance. 

Dietrick vs. Dietrick, 88 N. J. Eq. P. 560.

I now come to the question whether the wife should be granted further alimony in face of the lump sum settlement agreed to by

her, and approved by the Court, in view of the fact that she possesses a separate estate from which, however, she has not received, nor been entitled to receive, any income other than being furnished with proper living quarters. The husband contends that her corporate property assets within her control should and could have produced an income adequate for her support. The proof clearly shows otherwise. The financial status of the corporations in which she is interested appears to be about what could be expected in these times, where the sole source of income is from real estate which was developed and financed during the recent boom period. It appears that the properties of Walker Realty 

Company and Arlington Realty Company are heavily mortgaged, and are being managed considerably with permission of, and under the supervision of, the mortgagees. The taxes are in arrears. 

Even the husband admits that he received no interest upon a mortgage which he received from the Walker Realty Company covering its apartment house in Newark. If it can be said that the wife surrendered her interest in Arlington Realty Company to her son without justification, it was not prejudicial to the husband. 

The proofs show that concern has been conducted at a loss for the past few years. Whatever interest the wife may have in the 

Florida property is such that it avails her nothing. Under these circumstances, can it then be said that the wife is not entitled, under our law, to further maintenance from her husband? If not, then she has no recourse but to hypothecate or sell her separate estate in order to secure funds for her maintenance. I would have no hesitation in holding that she should first do so, if that were practicable. The wife would then only be doing equity. 

From the proofs, however, it fairly appears that it is not practicable for her to attempt to secure funds for her support by disposing of such separate estate as she has. Such equity as there may be in the various properties does not appear to be available in these times. I think the Court, in a case such as this, should take judicial notice of the fact that there is practically no market for the sale of property of this sort where it is heavily mortgaged and has been operated at a loss for some years past. The proofs fairly permit that inference. I have no question but that, as the husband contends, the wife's corporate interests are quite valuable. 

The value, however, is prospective. It is certainly not immediate. 

The question concerning her need for further support from her husband is immediate, and not prospective. Equitable, therefore, the capacity of her estate to furnish her support must be judged in light of its present availability for that purpose. As between the equity of compelling this wife first to have recourse to her

estate for her support, and the equity of compelling the husband to meet his duty in that respect by further payments to her despite the lump sum alimony settlement, I have no hesitation in holding that he is available for further allowance. Such is the reasonable import of the alimony section of our Divorce Act (supra). To decide otherwise is to deny the significance of the statutory prescription that the wife shall be entitled to such alimony as is fit, reasonable and just, and that the orders therein may be revised and altered from time to time as the circumstances may require. 

Baumgarten vs. Baumgarten, supra.

I find no proof of the charge that the wife, through her son, has adopted a course of procedure to strip the husband of everything he has owned by every available means. The proofs do show amply that the judgment of the parties thereto, and their children, of the value of the properties which they developed and were interested in, was erroneous as tested by the past few years. 

The present plight of the husband and the wife in that respect is chargeable entirely to circumstances quite beyond their control, which have resulted in their property interests being a burden rather than a benefit. I have no question but what the husband and the wife exercised their best judgment in perfecting the settlement of the alimony question by the lump sum payment pursuant to the order of January 31st, 1931, in this cause. Again, with the passage of time, economic conditions have nullified the efficacy of the provisions of that order for the wife's support. 

I have noted that the order providing for the payment of alimony in a lump sum in this case was entered as a final adjudication of that phase of the suit at a time when no step had been taken in the cause except for the filing of the petition for divorce. 

Process of citation was not served until October 15, 1932. That is a necessary step for jurisdiction. Henry vs. Henry, 79 N. J. 

Eq. 493, affirmed 81 Eq. 512. Can the defendant in a suit for divorce, by his consent, confer jurisdiction upon the Court to support the entry of an order for settlement of alimony by payment of a lump sum prior to jurisdiction having been acquired over him pursuant to our Divorce Act of 1907, by service of process? This question was not raised, however, and I deem it unnecessary to pass upon it.

In determining the sum which the wife is entitled to receive from her husband by way of further alimony, I conclude that it should be fixed in light of her present circumstances, the physical and social position of the parties, the husband's property and income and the separate income and property of the wife. Dietrick vs. Dietrick (supra). Another factor that must be con-

MARGERUM V. MARGERUM 

sidered is the fact that the wife received the benefit of the lump sum alimony settlement at the expense of the husband. Presently the wife's estate is such that it does not produce any income, nor is it reasonably available for her support, as I have already stated. She does have proper living quarters furnished her without expense. She is elderly and unqualified to earn a living. The husband, presently possessed of an unproductive estate, has a salary income of about $265.00 per month and is furnished with maintenance. Considering all of these factors, and the equities heretofore stated, until the further order of the Court, the wife is entitled to receive the sum of $10.00 per week from her husband as a further award for her support, payments to begin as of February 7, last. It follows that this order will be modified upon proof of change in essential circumstances of the wife's separate estate. I shall allow the wife the costs of the proceedings, but no counsel fee. 

This decision was affirmed in 118 N. J. Eq. 309, 178 Atl. 743 (1935).

CLARK P. MARGERUM, defendant.

ON FINAL HEARING 

The petition is for divorce. At the hearing leave was asked and consented to and granted to amend the petition by adding an additional count under the Infants Act, praying for custody of and support for the infant child of the marriage as between parents living separate and apart. By consent, the petition for divorce is to be dismissed and decree entered on the second count, with an allowance of $3.00 a week for the support of the child.

Report of the Commissioners Appointed to Attend the 

Uniform Divorce Law Congress as Delegates for the State of New Jersey. 

Submitted, January, 1907.

To His Excellency, Edward C. Stokes, Governor of the State of New Jersey.

The commissioners appointed to attend the Uniform Divorce Law Congress, as delegates for the State of New Jersey, respectfully submit the following report:

The assembling of this congress was one result of the general movement within the last few years for the restriction of the great and constantly increasing number of divorces in the United States. 

As to part of this increase in divorces, attended with special evils and scandals, there was a wide-spread and well-founded conviction that it was due to what has been characterized as "Migratory Divorces," where a misuse, or fraudulent use, is made by the residents of one State of the laws and courts of another State, for the purpose of obtaining divorces, which could not be secured. under the laws of their own State, and the suppression of divorces of this character was one of the principal reforms discussed. The power to establish a divorce law, uniform throughout the nation, has not been committed to the Federal Government by the constitution, and therefore any action in the direction of control by law must, in the absence of a Federal constitutional amendment, be secured by a co-operation of the States. 

President Roosevelt, in a message to the United States Congress of January 30, 1905, expressed the hope that such co-operation of the States could be secured, and Governor Pennypacker, acting on this suggestion of the President, by the authority of the Legislature of Pennsylvania, formally requested the co-operation of the other States in the assembling of a congress of delegates to consider the laws and decisions of the several States, with a view to the drafting of a general law to be submitted to the Legislatures of the States, securing, as nearly as might be possible, uniform statutes upon the subject of divorce throughout the nation. This congress, which convened at Washington, in February, 1906, was 1177

REPORT OF DELEGATES 

attended by delegates from forty States, besides the District of Columbia and one Territory, an attendance more general than had ever previously occurred at any purely voluntary convention of representatives or delegates of the States for any purpose. The congress, after a four days' session, devoted exclusively to the discussion and settlement of the principles upon which uniform action seemed to be practicable, adopted a series of resolutions expressing these principles, and directed them to be embodied in a law to be submitted at an adjourned meeting. Such meeting was held in 

November, 1906, at Philadelphia, and after two days' discussion the form or draft of the proposed law was finally settled. 

The congress also directed its committee on resolutions to prepare an address in its behalf to the President and Congress and to the Governors and Legislatures of the several States, calling the attention of these officers and legislative bodies to the several provisions of the Uniform Divorce law, and the reasons for their adoption. This address, together with the resolutions and the law, are annexed to this report as Schedule (1), (2) and (3).

The commissioners have also, at the request of your Excellency, prepared a revision of the Divorce law of this State, incorporating such of the provisions of the Uniform Divorce law as were recommended for adoption by every State, and making the necessary changes in our present law. This proposed revision is also annexed hereto as Schedule No. 4.

In submitting this Uniform Divorce law and the proposed New 

Jersey revision for such action, and recommendation as your

Excellency may deem advisable, we desire to emphasize especially some important considerations. The first is that the present adoption in all of the States of that portion of the law prescribing the causes for annulment and absolute divorce is not expected or even recommended by the Divorce Congress. It fully recognized that the sovereign right of each State to regulate the status of its own citizens, and the conflict of views in the communities of the different States on the subject of the causes of divorce precludes any universal agreement on the subject of causes of divorce at the present time. The Divorce Congress, therefore, while adopting or enumerating certain causes as a maximum standard, being the causes which are in accordance with the legislation of a large number of the States, did this with the recommendation that no additional causes be recognized by any State, and with the declaration that where the causes are now restricted within this number prescribed by the Uniform Divorce law, no change in the present statute is called for.

In preparing the revised New Jersey statute, the causes for

UNIFORM DIVORCE CONGRESS 

1179 annulment of marriage and for absolute divorce from the bonds of matrimony remain, therefore, without change with one exception-this is the addition of a provision for annulment of marriages contracted under the age of sixteen for girls and the age of eighteen for boys, which may be annuled at the suit of the injured party only, unless confirmed by such party arriving at these respective ages. This provision was adopted at the adjourned session of the congress and the reasons for it are shortly given in the following extract from the address: "Each State fixes by statute or decision some limit of age, and these ages fixed by the act, while raising the limits fixed by marriages at common law, are not higher than the age fixed by statutes in many States, protecting females against consent to intercourse. 

The social conditions now generally existing through the Union do not seem to be such as to call for the encouragement of marriages at an earlier age, and the evils likely to result generally from such immature marriages seem to require their absolute prohibition." 

The second suggestion is that the most important part of the work of the Divorce Congress, and that to which most of its discussions were directed, related to the general subject of the jurisdiction of the courts of a State to grant decrees of absolute divorce and to the effect to be given in one State to decrees of divorce obtained in another. Common action by the several States upon these two subjects and the recognition of common principles based on natural justice, is now absolutely necessary, not only to root out the scandals and evils of "Migratory Divorces," but also to establish a uniform law in reference to the effect of decrees of other States in all cases not covered by the Federal Constitution, as interpreted by the Supreme Court. By the latest decision of the United States Supreme Court, rendered in April, 1906 (Haddock v. Haddock, 201 U. S. Rep. 562), it was declared that the faith and credit to be given by one State to the decrees of divorce obtained in another, where the court did not have jurisdiction over both parties, depended solely upon the laws of comity recognized in each State and did not come within the protection of the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution, unless the action was brought and the divorce obtained in the State of the matrimonial domicile and (it would seem) by the innocent party who remained there.

As to the effect of this decision and the necessity of uniform State action, the address of the Divorce Congress says: "This rule removes from the protection of the Federal Constitution and the establishment of a uniform rule thereunder all that class of cases where either the innocent party or both parties have

REPORT OF DELEGATES 

removed from the matrimonial domicile to another State and have become bona fide residents thereof. To establish a uniform law which shall reach all cases not covered by the United States Supreme Court decisions, and remove as far as possible the scandal to public morals, as well as the reproach to American jurisprudence, arising from a man and a woman being held to be married in one State and not married in another, the congress adopted two principles or rules, one relating to jurisdiction over defendants not personally served with process in the State in which action is brought, the other relating to the effect of foreign decrees."

Jurisdiction for divorce against non-residents not actually served with process in this State has long been exercised in New Jersey, but under restrictions imposed by statute and rules of court which are intended to give to the non-resident defendant, if practicable, notice of the suit and an opportunity to defend it. 

And our decisions, giving to other States the same right and privilege, have also, on the grounds of comity, recognized the binding effect of decrees obtained in other States against non-residents, when there was such notice of the suit and opportunity to defend. 

Mere publication, however, without actual notice (if actual notice was practicable), has not, in this State, been held sufficient foundation for a decree of divorce against a non-resident. 

The provisions of the Uniform Divorce law, in respect to jurisdiction, are based substantially on the same principles as the present law and practice in New Jersey, except that the Uniform law provides for personal service of notice of the suit, both within and without the State, whenever practicable, leaving it to the States to prescribe by statutes or rules of court for a substituted service in case personal service cannot be effected. And in all cases of substituted service, publication of the notice of the suit must be made, the purpose of this being to assure, as far as possible, notice of the suit to the defendant-if he is not personally served.

The commission earnestly recommended the adoption of the provisions of the Uniform Divorce law relating to jurisdiction and to the effect of foreign decrees as the vital portions of the proposed law, and they believe that their general adoption will mark a practical advance in the direction of that reformation of the Divorce law which is now the duty of the States as well as their right.

The sections relating to jurisdiction are 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the Uniform Divorce law, and sections 5, 6 and 7 of the proposed 

New Jersey revision. [Now 1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-9; 2:50-10;

UNIFORM DIVORCE CONGRESS 

1181 2:50-11]. In substance they provide for a bona fide residence in this State of one of the parties to the action for at least two years (except in cases of adultery) when the cause for action arose in this State, and for a like term of residence of one of the parties in this State when either has become a resident of this State since the cause of action arose, with the important proviso in the latter case that the cause of action must have been recognized in the State in which such party resided at the time the cause of action arose, as a ground for the same relief asked in the suit. 

The proviso was intended to meet the "Migratory Divorce" evil, and it was adopted unanimously by the delegates to the congress as one effective step toward the suppression of these divorces. The provisions as to the effect of final decrees are section 22 of the Uniform Divorce law and section 36 of the pro posed New Jersey revision. [Now 1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-35]. They provide that full faith and credit shall be given in all courts of this State to a decree of annulment of marriage or divorce obtained in another State when the jurisdiction of the court was obtained in the manner and in substantial conformity with the conditions prescribed by the sections of the act relating to jurisdiction, but with the special proviso "that if any inhabitant of this State shall go into another State, Territory or country in order to obtain a decree of divorce for a cause which occurred while the parties resided in this State, or for a cause which is not ground for a divorce under the laws of this State, a decree so obtained shall be of no force or effect in this State." 

This is a statutory provision that has long been in force in Massachusetts, and was unanimously adopted by the congress as another and probably the most effective remedy for "Migratory Divorces." The validity of the statute has been expressly affirmed by the United States Supreme Court (Andrews v. Andrews, 188 

U. S. Rep. 14 (1903), and the substantial unanimity with which these provisions, as to jurisdiction and foreign decrees, were adopted, after full discussion and deliberation by the Divorce Congress, encourages the belief that they may be adopted by all of the States, or by so many of them as to go a long way toward the reformation in one important direction of the American laws relating to marriage and divorce. 

It remains for the commissioners to call attention to some other changes which the Uniform Divorce law makes in our present law, and which are submitted for the action of the States. The first is the provision allowing limited divorces from bed and board, as well as absolute divorce for the same causes (adultery and desertion), at the option of the injured party, who is not to

REPORT OF DELEGATES 

be compelled to ask for a dissolution of the marriage. This option, as the address states, "will extend the relief of limited divorce to a large and increasing class, who, on account of religious beliefs, conscientious scruples or other sufficient reason, would not seek absolute divorce, and are therefore barred in many cases from a proper relief by legal or judicial separation. 

In New Jersey, a statute was passed in 1891 (Pamph. L., p. 76; 

2 Gen. Stat., p. 1274) allowing persons who had conscientious scruples against absolute divorce to obtain limited divorces in lieu thereof, and for the same causes. This law was, however, declared unconstitutional by the Court of Errors and Appeals, in 

1896 (Middleton v. Middleton, 9 Dick. Ch. Rep. 692), because it gave special privileges to a class of persons selected on the basis of their private opinions on the subject of absolute divorce. The proposed statute (section 3, New Jersey Revision) remedies this defect by giving the option to every injured party to procure a limited divorce for adultery and desertion. Under our present law a limited divorce is granted only for extreme cruelty. 

Another provision of the Uniform Divorce law changing our existing law is the one providing that at the hearing of suits for absolute divorce the decree made in the first instance shall be only a decree nisi, and that this shall not become absolute until after a year. (Sections 16 and 17, Uniform Divorce law, and sections 

23 and 24, New Jersey Revision. [Now 1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-29; 

2:50-30]). This law has worked favorably in the few States where it has been adopted, and the congress recommends its trial in other States. If adopted, it would be some protection against the obtaining of decrees of divorce by collusion or fraud, and prevent the scandalous haste in remarriages which sometimes occur. Another change relates to the manner of hearing undefended cases, which at present are disposed of by a special master on evidence usually taken in his office. Contested cases are now, almost without exception, heard publicly before a Vice Chancellor, although parties may still, if neither desires a trial before a Vice Chancellor, take the evidence in a master's office and bring the cause to hearing upon deposition so taken. The Uniform Divorce law (section 12) and the New Jersey revision (section 17) requires the hearings in all cases, undefended as well as defended, to be in open court, and if adopted in our practice will require all divorce cases to be heard before the Chancellor, or a Vice Chancellor, or Advisory Master.

The remaining changes relate purely to matters of procedure or practice, such as the appointment of solicitors to defend uncontested cases if the court deems it proper; the prohibition against

UNIFORM DIVORCE CONGRESS 

1183 impounding the record or evidence or refusing access thereto, and the requirement of proof aside from the defendant's admissions in order to grant decrees of nullity or divorce. These provisions were incorporated in the Uniform Divorce law for the purpose, mainly, of meeting lax conditions in the administration of the divorce laws, which were thought to exist in many of the States, but are not specially called for in this State. We have included them in the proposed New Jersey revision, and submit them with the suggestion that as they are not considered by the commissioners essential parts of the Uniform Divorce law so far as this State is concerned, their rejection-if they be considered unnecessary or inadvisable-will not affect the general object of the uniform law.

In the proposed New Jersey revision is included one change in our procedure, made after conference with the Chancellor. This change (made by section 10, New Jersey Revision [now 1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-22]) requires all divorce and nullity suits brought under the act to be by petition only. Under the present practice two methods are allowed-either bill or petition. There appears to be no good reason for continuing this double procedure, and as the proceeding by petition is the simplest and least expensive, this method is selected for all suits under the act. 

All of which is respectfully submitted, JOHN R. EMERY,

The following sections of the draft act were not incorporated in the act as passed by the Legislature: 

17. [All hearings and trials in causes arising under this act shall be had in open court before the Chancellor or Vice Chancellor or Advisory Master, and shall in all cases be public.] 

21. [No decree for annulment of marriage, or for divorce shall be granted unless the cause is shown by affirmative proof aside from any admissions on the part of the defendant.] 

22. [No record or evidence in any case shall be impounded, or access thereto refused.]

p. 242 

Refusal of Sexual Relations; Impotence. 

In a suit for divorce for desertion premised upon the husband's refusal and neglect to consummate the marriage after nine years of cohabitation, the court ordered an inspection to ascertain whether or not the husband was potent. The husband's answer to the charge of desertion was that he was physically incapable of consummating the marriage. 

Thiesmeier v. Thiesmeier, Dk 126-192 (1938). 

§ 268. 

p. 325 

Order of Publication and Notice Thereof. 

Form of notice. Under an order for publication in a divorce suit substituted service of the requisite papers was made upon the defendant by registered mail resulting in a return card being received signed by the defendant personally. Due publication was made under the order of the notice in the form prescribed by Rule 36 except that in the body of the notice the petitioner's name was set forth as Elizabeth Huyler (her maiden name) instead of Elizabeth Huyler Campbell, her marriage name and the name in which suit had been instituted. 

The court held that the form of the notice constituted substantial compliance with Rule 36. 

Campbell v. Campbell, Dk 126-186 (1938).

Effect of Award in Gross on Subsequent Applica- 

A lump sum settlement given by the husband to his wife while they were residing in the State of New York has been held not to be a bar to an award of alimony in a subsequent suit by the wife for divorce in this state. 

Polyckronos v. Polyckronos, Dk 117-337 (Sept. 19, 1938) [probably to be published]. 

An agreement in lieu of alimony executed after decree nisi and before entry of the final decree and not approved by the court does not bar a subsequent allowance. The court, however, was of the opinion that had the agreement been approved by the court, the husband must respond in alimony in view of the wife's destitution.

Parmly v. Parmly, 16 N. J. Misc. 447, (Sept. 21, 1938).

Revision of Order. Proceedings to effect the revision of a decree for alimony may be initiated by petition and not by bill of review.

Parmly v. Parmly, 16 N. J. Misc. 447, 450, (Sept. 21, 1938).

§ 487. Enforcing the Agreement in Chancery and at Law. 

An agreement between husband and wife, executed in New York, whereby the husband agreed to pay his wife the sum of $15.00 per week has been held to be enforceable in the Court of Chancery. 

Meyer v. Meyer, 124 N. J. Eq. 198, 1 Atl. (2d) 4 (1938).
